class.name: CameraAttributes
class.description: Controls camera-specific attributes such as depth of field, exposure override, white balance, grain and the camera's LUT. When used in a [WorldEnvironment] it provides default settings for exposure, auto-exposure, white balance, grain, LUT, and depth of field that will be used by all cameras without their own [CameraAttributes], including the editor camera. When used in a [Camera3D] it will override any [CameraAttributes] set in the [WorldEnvironment]. When used in [VoxelGI] or [LightmapGI], only the exposure settings will be used. See also [Environment] for general 3D environment settings. This is a pure virtual class that is inherited by [CameraAttributesPhysical] and [CameraAttributesPractical].

members.member: If [code]true[/code], enables the tonemapping auto exposure mode of the scene renderer. If [code]true[/code], the renderer will automatically determine the exposure setting to adapt to the scene's illumination and the observed light. [b]Note:[/b] Auto-exposure is only supported in the Forward+ rendering method, not Mobile or Compatibility.
The scale of the auto exposure effect. Affects the intensity of auto exposure.
The speed of the auto exposure effect. Affects the time needed for the camera to perform auto exposure.

If [code]true[/code], the lens images each color at a slightly different size (lateral chromatic aberration), so edges get red and blue/cyan fringes that grow toward the frame's edges. [b]Note:[/b] Lateral chromatic aberration does not depend on the aperture on a real lens, so stopping down does not reduce it here either. In the Compatibility renderer it makes the scene go through the post-processing pass.

The size difference between the colors. At [code]1.0[/code] red and blue are spread by 0.1% of the distance from the center, a moderate amount for a real lens (about one pixel at the corners of a 1080p image). Negative values swap the colors' order.

If [code]true[/code], barrel distortion zooms in just enough that no border from outside the rendered image shows, as cameras do when they correct their lenses. If [code]false[/code], what lies outside the rendered image is black.

If [code]true[/code], [CameraAttributesPhysical] takes the distortion of a typical rectilinear lens of its focal length and sensor (about 5% barrel at 14 mm on full frame, 2% at 24 mm, none around 50-60 mm, a slight pincushion on short telephotos) instead of [member distortion_k1] and [member distortion_k2]. An anamorphic lens ([member CameraAttributesPhysical.lens_anamorphic_squeeze]) distorts more horizontally. Not used by [CameraAttributesPractical].

If [code]true[/code], the lens bends straight lines: barrel distortion bows them outward (typical of wide-angle lenses), pincushion distortion inward (typical of telephoto lenses). The image is resampled by the tonemap pass, glow included. [b]Note:[/b] Effects that run before tonemapping (depth of field, screen-space reflections, SMAA's input) see the undistorted image, as they would on a real camera's sensor data, apart from FXAA, which follows the distortion. In the Compatibility renderer it makes the scene go through the post-processing pass.

The first radial coefficient of the Brown-Conrady model, which moves a point at distance [code]r[/code] from the center (1 at the frame's corners) to [code]r * (1 + k1 * r² + k2 * r⁴)[/code]. Negative values give barrel distortion, positive values pincushion: [code]-0.05[/code] pulls the corners 5% toward the center.

The second radial coefficient of the Brown-Conrady model (see [member distortion_k1]), which acts mostly near the corners. Opposite signs of [member distortion_k1] and [member distortion_k2] give the "mustache" distortion of some wide-angle lenses.
Multiplier for the exposure amount. A higher value results in a brighter image.

Sensitivity of camera sensors, measured in ISO. A higher sensitivity results in a brighter image. If [member auto_exposure_enabled] is [code]true[/code], this can be used as a method of exposure compensation, doubling the value will increase the exposure value (measured in EV100) by 1 stop. The sensitivity also sets the film speed or sensor gain of [member grain_enabled]: higher values give coarser, stronger grain or noise. [b]Note:[/b] Exposure is only affected when [member ProjectSettings.rendering/lights_and_shadows/use_physical_light_units] is enabled. Otherwise, this property only affects grain, and is only shown in the inspector while grain is enabled.

If [code]true[/code], the camera adds film grain or digital sensor noise, depending on [member grain_type], modeled on a 36×24 mm frame at the ISO given by [member exposure_sensitivity]. The grain is sized and scaled for the resolution it is drawn at, following Selwyn's law: a lower resolution shows weaker, coarser noise per pixel, so the image looks equally grainy at any resolution. A new grain pattern is drawn every frame. Grain is applied in linear scene-referred color after exposure and white balance, before tonemapping, so the tonemapper compresses it in the highlights as a print or a camera's tone curve does. It is not drawn in reflection probes or the viewport's debug draw modes. [b]Note:[/b] When 3D resolution scaling uses FSR 1.0 or SMAA is enabled, the grain is drawn at the 3D resolution and upscaled with the image. In the Compatibility rendering method, enabling grain enables the post-processing pass.
Multiplier for the grain's amplitude. At [code]1.0[/code], the amount is the one modeled for the film or sensor at [member exposure_sensitivity]. [code]0.0[/code] disables grain.

Multiplier for the size of the grain (or of the noise's structure for [constant GRAIN_TYPE_DIGITAL]). Each grain keeps its contrast, so larger grain is also more visible. At [code]1.0[/code], the size is the one modeled for the film or sensor at [member exposure_sensitivity].
The kind of grain or noise to simulate. See [enum GrainType] for options.

If [code]true[/code], the camera applies [member lut_texture], a look-up table, the way a camera applies a LUT to its monitoring or recorded image. It is applied before the [Environment]'s adjustments, so [member Environment.adjustment_color_correction] grades the result. [b]Note:[/b] Not applied in the viewport's debug draw modes or in reflection probes. In the Compatibility rendering method, enabling a LUT enables the post-processing pass.

What the LUT expects as its input. [constant LUT_INPUT_DISPLAY] is for creative or "look" LUTs made for Rec.709/sRGB images. The camera log encodings are for LUTs made for that camera's log footage, such as the manufacturer's "log to Rec.709" LUTs: the scene is converted to that camera's gamut and log curve, the LUT turns it into the displayed image, and [member Environment.tonemap_mode] is not used. Set exposure so middle gray is where the camera expects it, as you would on set. See [enum LUTInput] for options.

How much of the LUT's result is used, from [code]0.0[/code] (none) to [code]1.0[/code]. Blends between the image without the LUT (for a log input, the [Environment]'s tonemapper) and the LUT's output, in sRGB-encoded values as grading tools do.

The look-up table, a [Texture3D] indexed by red (width), green (height) and blue (depth), whose texel centers hold the output for inputs evenly spaced from [code]0.0[/code] to [code]1.0[/code]. Adobe/Resolve [code].cube[/code] files (3D, 1D, or a 1D shaper followed by a 3D table) are imported as such a texture automatically.

If [code]true[/code], the lens darkens the image toward the frame's edges. With [CameraAttributesPhysical] the darkening follows the lens: natural vignetting, the cos⁴ law of the field angle from [member CameraAttributesPhysical.frustum_focal_length] and the sensor, plus optical vignetting, where the lens barrel clips the aperture off-axis, which is strongest wide open (at [member CameraAttributesPhysical.lens_max_aperture]) and gone two stops down. With [CameraAttributesPractical] it is a free curve set by [member vignetting_strength] and [member vignetting_falloff]. [b]Note:[/b] Vignetting is applied by the tonemap pass to scene light before white balance, grain and tonemapping, in all renderers. In the Compatibility renderer it makes the scene go through the post-processing pass.

How the darkening of [CameraAttributesPractical] grows from the center: it is [member vignetting_strength] stops times the distance from the center (1 at the corners) raised to this power. Higher values keep the center bright and darken only the corners. Not used by [CameraAttributesPhysical], whose falloff comes from the lens.

With [CameraAttributesPhysical], scales the lens's own vignetting in stops: [code]1.0[/code] is the physical amount, [code]2.0[/code] doubles the darkening in stops, [code]0.0[/code] removes it. With [CameraAttributesPractical], the darkening at the frame's corners in stops.

The color temperature, in Kelvin, of the light the camera is balanced for, from [code]2000.0[/code] to [code]10000.0[/code]. A light of this temperature appears the way a 6500 K light does at the default setting: lower values turn the image blue and make warm (tungsten, candle) lighting look neutral, higher values turn it orange and make cool (overcast, shade) lighting look neutral. At [code]6500.0[/code] with a [member white_balance_tint] of [code]0.0[/code], white balance is skipped entirely and the image is unchanged. The illuminant is taken on the Planckian locus with the same approximation [member Light3D.light_temperature] uses, so a light set to a given temperature renders neutral under a white balance of the same temperature. The adaptation is a von Kries transform in Bradford cone space, applied in linear scene-referred color after exposure and before tonemapping. [b]Note:[/b] Unlike [member exposure_sensitivity], this works whether or not [member ProjectSettings.rendering/lights_and_shadows/use_physical_light_units] is enabled, in every rendering method.

Green-magenta correction of the white balance, from [code]-150.0[/code] to [code]150.0[/code]. It moves the assumed illuminant perpendicular to the Planckian locus by [code]1/3000[/code] Duv per unit, so the full range is [code]0.05[/code] Duv either way: a positive value compensates for a green illuminant and turns the image magenta, a negative value compensates for a magenta one and turns it green, as the tint slider of most raw converters does.

constants.constant: Color negative film grain. Its granularity follows Kodak's published RMS granularity across film speeds (8 at ISO 100, about 11 at ISO 400, 18 at ISO 3200) and grows with the square root of the negative's density, so the grain is strongest in the midtones and fades in deep shadows and, once tonemapped, in the highlights. Each dye layer grains partly on its own, giving the grain a little color. This is the most realistic option for a filmic look.
Black-and-white film grain: the same model as [constant GRAIN_TYPE_FILM], driven by luminance, with no color in the grain.

Digital sensor noise from a full-frame sensor with 6 µm photosites: photon shot noise, which grows with the square root of the light captured, plus read noise, which dominates the shadows, per Bayer color channel. As on a real camera, it is invisible at low ISO and shows from about ISO 1600. With [member auto_exposure_enabled], auto exposure acts as sensor gain (auto ISO): a dark scene brightened by auto exposure gets noisier.

The LUT takes the tonemapped image, sRGB-encoded, and returns an sRGB-encoded image. Applied after tonemapping and glow. The LUT's range is SDR: with HDR output, brighter values are clipped to [code]1.0[/code].
ARRI LogC3 (EI 800) in ARRI Wide Gamut 3: for LUTs made for ALEXA footage.
ACEScct in ACES AP1 primaries, adapted from D65 with Bradford.
Represents the size of the [enum LUTInput] enum.
